narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 64% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the review treated first-time bar failure as more likely than success, which led to rejection.

The most influential factor was your year-three class-rank decile of 1, far below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students. This was the strongest signal and pushed the prediction toward failure. The second most important factor was your LSAT score of 19, well below the accepted-student average of about 37; it also pushed toward failure. The third was your year-one class-rank decile of 1, again far below the accepted-student average of about 6, and it reinforced the same direction. Together, these academic and admissions indicators outweighed other information. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To improve your next application, focus on the areas the review treated as most predictive. Prepare for and retake the LSAT, aiming for a score closer to competitive applicants. Meet with an academic advisor to discuss your grades, whether additional coursework or a graduate record could strengthen your file, and how to document improvement. Ask admissions offices for feedback, apply to a balanced list of programs where your credentials fit, and begin bar-exam planning early. The denial reflects a predicted risk based on the information available, not a final judgment of your ability.
